To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the trustworthiness criteria are useful for assessing the quality of qualitative inquiry, but that the authenticity criteria are not useful for this purpose.

(a) naturalistic evaluators should be aware of and use both trustworthiness and authenticity criteria; (b) trustworthiness criteria are more important than authenticity criteria; (c) trustworthiness and authentic criteria can be combined into an evaluation matrix; and (d) the use of trustworthiness and/or authenticity criteria is more likely to lead to the production of trustworthy and authentic naturalistic evaluations

(a) the trustworthiness criteria of dependability, credibility, and confirmability parallel the conventional criteria of reliability, validity, and objectivity, and (b) the authenticity criteria of coherence, resonance, and practicality are implied directly by the assumptions of naturalistic inquiry
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of rigorous naturalistic criteria to the evaluation of a program for the prevention of child abuse.
the development of an evaluation methodology which is both rigorous and authentic.
the question of how to evaluate rigor in naturalistic inquiry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the naturalistic approach is rigorous, but that it is rigorous in different ways than the conventional approach.
the trustworthiness criteria are the most important, but the authenticity criteria are the most fundamental.
the trustworthiness and authenticity criteria, taken together, are sufficient and appropriate for naturalistic inquiry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to develop a new paradigm for evaluation.
naturalistic evaluation is rigorous and that it has a place in the evaluation field.
the new paradigm of evaluation is rigorous and trustworthy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the new paradigm of inquiry has not yet been fully developed, and we suggest a number of areas where further development is necessary, especially in the areas of authenticity criteria.
naturalistic evaluators need not be concerned that the new paradigm will lead to a loss of rigor.
naturalistic evaluation can be rigorous and trustworthy.
